title: The Shepherd and the Wolf
summary: A young shepherd who jokes that a wolf is attacking his flock learns that lying costs him people's trust, especially on the evening a real wolf finally appears.
poll: It is okay to tell a lie as a joke, even if it worries other people.

versions.title: The Boy and the Wolf
versions.text:
Samir was a shepherd boy.
He had a flock of sheep.
He kept them on a hill.
The hill was near his village.

Each day, Samir sat with the flock.
It was quiet there.
He got bored.
He got lonely too.

One day, Samir had an idea.
He ran to the village.
He yelled, "A wolf! A wolf!"
The people ran to help him.
But there was no wolf.
Samir just laughed.

Samir did the same trick two more times.
Each time, the people ran up the hill.
Each time, there was no wolf.
The people got mad.
They did not trust him now.

One night, a real wolf came near the flock.
Samir called for help.
No one came.
They thought it was just a joke.

Samir's dog barked and barked.
This time, Samir told the truth.
He did not yell silly things.
Some people heard the dog.
They ran up with sticks.
They made a lot of noise.
The wolf ran away.
No sheep were hurt.

Samir learned that the truth matters.
From then on, he was honest.

versions.title: The Shepherd and the Wolf
versions.text:
Samir was a young shepherd boy who lived near a small village.

Every day, he led his flock of sheep up a grassy hill. They grazed there for hours.

Watching the flock alone was quiet work. Samir often felt bored and lonely. He had no one to talk to.

One afternoon, Samir decided to play a trick. He ran down to the village. He shouted, "A wolf! A wolf is attacking my sheep!" The villagers dropped their work at once. They hurried up the hill to help him. But there was no wolf in sight. Samir simply laughed at how easily he had fooled them.

Feeling pleased with himself, Samir played the same trick twice more. Each time, the villagers rushed up the hill. Each time, they found nothing but a grinning boy and a calm flock. Slowly, the villagers grew angry. They stopped believing Samir's warnings.

One evening, as the light faded, a real wolf crept toward the flock. Samir shouted for help as loudly as he could. But no one came running this time. The villagers thought it was simply another one of his jokes.

Samir's dog began barking wildly. This time, instead of exaggerating, Samir spoke the plain truth in a steady voice. A few villagers noticed the strange, urgent barking. They climbed the hill with sticks and noise. Startled, the wolf turned and fled. Not a single sheep was harmed.

From that day forward, Samir understood that the truth truly matters. The village slowly learned to trust him once again.

versions.title: The Shepherd and the Wolf
versions.text:
Samir was a young shepherd boy. He lived at the edge of a quiet village in a dry, hilly region. Every morning, he led his family's flock of sheep up a grassy slope, where they grazed for most of the day.

Spending so many hours alone with the flock was tiring, repetitive work. Samir often felt bored and lonely. Nobody was nearby to talk to or warn him as the hours dragged on.

One dull afternoon, Samir decided to play a trick on the villagers just to break the monotony. He dashed down the hill shouting, "A wolf! A wolf is attacking my sheep!" The villagers dropped their tools at once. They rushed up the hill in a small panic to rescue him. But when they arrived, there was no wolf anywhere in sight. Samir simply burst out laughing at how easily he had fooled the whole village.

Feeling pleased with himself, Samir repeated the same trick two more times over the following weeks. Each time, he sent the villagers into another needless panic. Each time, they found nothing but a grinning boy beside a calm flock. Little by little, the villagers grew tired and resentful. They finally decided to ignore Samir's cries altogether. They no longer trusted a single word he said.

One evening, as the light faded, a real wolf crept quietly toward the unguarded flock. Terrified, Samir shouted for help as loudly as he could. But nobody came running this time. The villagers remembered his old tricks and simply chose to ignore him again.

Samir's loyal sheepdog began barking wildly and refused to stop. This time, rather than exaggerating, Samir forced himself to stay calm. He spoke the plain truth in a steady voice. A few curious villagers finally noticed how urgent the barking sounded. They climbed the hill carrying sticks and torches, making a great deal of noise. Startled, the wolf turned and fled into the darkness. Not a single sheep was harmed.

From that day forward, Samir understood that honesty and trust, once broken, take real effort to rebuild. The village slowly learned to believe him again.

In a dry, hilly region of the countryside, where water was scarce and the land offered little beyond coarse grass for grazing, a young shepherd boy named Samir lived at the edge of a quiet village and spent his mornings leading his family's flock of sheep up a grassy slope, where the animals grazed for most of the day beneath the open sky while he kept watch alone, hour after hour, with little to occupy his restless mind.

A wolf is attacking my sheep!" and watched, laughing, as the villagers abandoned their chores and rushed up in genuine alarm only to find no wolf at all, and himself delighted at how easily a single dramatic shout had managed to mislead an entire village.

Emboldened by this misleading success, Samir repeated the trick twice more over the following weeks, sending the villagers scrambling up the hill each time in another needless alarm, and each time they discovered nothing but a grinning boy beside an undisturbed flock; gradually, their patience wore thin, their trust eroded, and they resolved to ignore his cries altogether, unwilling to extend him any further credibility no matter how urgent his warnings sounded.

What finally changed their minds was not Samir's shouting but his dog, which began barking wildly and would not stop; unlike its young master, the dog had always been vigilant and had never once raised a false alarm over nothing, so its urgent, unbroken barking that evening unmistakably signaled real danger, and Samir, abandoning exaggeration entirely, forced himself to speak the plain, unembellished truth in a calm, steady voice, trying desperately to sound like an entirely different boy than the one who had lied so carelessly before.

Eventually, a few curious villagers noticed how strangely insistent the barking sounded and, despite their lingering doubts, climbed the hill carrying sticks and torches and making a great deal of noise as they approached; startled by the sudden commotion, the wolf turned sharply and vanished into the darkness, leaving every single sheep unharmed.

From that evening onward, Samir understood, more deeply than any lecture could have taught him, that honesty and credibility, once squandered through careless lies, cannot be restored overnight but must be earned back slowly, one honest day at a time, until his word in the village finally came to mean something once again.

keyWords.definition: a person whose job is to take care of sheep
keyWords.example: The young shepherd led his sheep to the river to drink.

keyWords.definition: a group of sheep, birds, or other animals that stay together
keyWords.example: A flock of sheep grazed quietly on the hillside.

keyWords.definition: a small group of homes where people live, smaller than a town
keyWords.example: Everyone in the small village knew each other by name.

keyWords.definition: a wild animal that looks like a large dog and can hunt other animals
keyWords.example: The farmers built a strong fence to keep the wolf away from their goats.

keyWords.definition: something that is true and really happened, not a lie
keyWords.example: Even though she was scared, Mona told her mother the truth about the broken vase.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A boy who learns that lying slowly costs him people's trust
A boy who searches every hillside for a missing young lamb
A village that decides to move to a cooler, shadier hill
A clever sheepdog that runs away to live in a nearby forest
questions.why: The story follows Samir as he jokes about a wolf, loses the village's trust, and then learns why honesty matters.

wrong.B: The story is not about a missing lamb.
wrong.C: The village does not move to a new hill in the story.
wrong.D: The sheepdog stays with Samir the whole story; it does not run away.

questions.stem: Why did Samir first shout that a wolf was attacking his sheep?
options: He wanted the villagers to bring him food and fresh water
He was bored and wanted to watch the villagers run up the hill
He thought he truly saw a wolf hiding near his flock
His sheepdog barked loudly and told him to call for help
questions.why: The story says Samir was bored and lonely, so he played the trick just to see the villagers come running.

wrong.A: The story does not say he wanted food or water.
wrong.C: There was no wolf at all the first time he shouted.
wrong.D: The dog does not give Samir the idea for the trick.

questions.stem: What did the villagers find when they ran up the hill the first time?
options: A real wolf that was chasing one of the frightened sheep
The sheep had wandered far away and gotten lost
No wolf at all, just Samir laughing beside his flock
Samir's sheepdog lying hurt near the grassy slope
questions.why: The story says there was no wolf in sight, and Samir simply laughed at how easily he had fooled them.

wrong.A: There was no wolf there at all the first time.
wrong.B: The sheep were still calmly with Samir, not lost.
wrong.D: The sheepdog was not hurt in the story.

questions.stem: What happened after Samir played the same trick two more times?
options: The villagers gave Samir a brand-new sheepdog
A wolf attacked the flock again immediately
Samir decided to move away to a new village
The villagers grew angry and stopped trusting him
questions.why: The story says that after the repeated tricks, the villagers became angry and stopped believing Samir's warnings.

wrong.A: No new dog is given to Samir in the story.
wrong.B: No wolf appears right after the repeated tricks.
wrong.C: Samir does not move to a new village.

questions.stem: Why did no one come when Samir called for help the night a real wolf came?
options: The villagers believed it was just another one of his jokes
All of the villagers were asleep and could not hear him
Samir's sheepdog had suddenly stopped barking at the wolf
Samir did not call out loudly enough for anyone to hear
questions.why: The story explains that the villagers assumed it was simply another one of his tiresome jokes, so nobody came.

wrong.B: The story does not say the villagers were asleep.
wrong.C: The dog kept barking wildly and would not stop.
wrong.D: Samir shouted as loudly as he possibly could.

questions.stem: Why did some villagers finally decide to check on Samir that night?
options: Samir had promised to pay them for coming to help
They had already seen the wolf from far down the road
It happened to be the usual time for the evening meal
The dog's barking sounded far more urgent than before
questions.why: The dog's barking was unusually urgent and would not stop, which is what finally made a few villagers notice and investigate.

wrong.A: Samir does not promise any payment in the story.
wrong.B: They had not seen the wolf themselves before climbing the hill.
wrong.C: Mealtime is never mentioned as the reason they came.

questions.stem: In the story, what does it mean that the wolf 'fled' into the darkness?
options: The wolf fell asleep near the edge of the dark forest
The wolf ran away quickly, scared by the sudden noise
The wolf stayed close by, watching the flock quietly
The wolf hid quietly under a large, flat rock nearby
questions.why: The story says the wolf was startled by the noise and turned and ran away into the dark, which is what fled means.

wrong.A: The wolf did not fall asleep; it ran off.
wrong.C: The wolf left the area instead of staying nearby.
wrong.D: The story does not say the wolf hid under a rock.

questions.stem: Why does the story end by saying the village slowly learned to trust Samir again?
options: To show that villagers in the story forget things quickly
To explain in detail how real wolves usually behave
To show that trust can be rebuilt through honesty over time
To tell readers that Samir received a special reward
questions.why: The ending shows that because Samir stayed honest, the village came to trust him again, teaching that honesty rebuilds trust.

wrong.A: The villagers remember his earlier tricks; they do not simply forget.
wrong.B: The story is not meant to teach facts about real wolves.
wrong.D: Samir does not receive any special reward in the story.

LOW.prompt: Do you think Samir was right to play a trick on the villagers? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think about Samir's trick.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I do not think Samir was right to play the trick. He shouted that a wolf was attacking his sheep when there was no wolf at all, and the villagers dropped their work to rescue him for nothing. Because he fooled them so many times, the villagers stopped believing him, so when a real wolf came, nobody came to help him right away. It was only his dog's barking that finally made a few villagers check on him.

keyWords.definition: to choose not to pay attention to something
keyWords.example: My brother tried to ignore the loud music and keep reading.

keyWords.definition: to tell someone about a danger before it happens
keyWords.example: The lifeguard warned the swimmers about the strong current.

keyWords.definition: a sudden feeling of fear that makes people act without thinking clearly
keyWords.example: The fire alarm caused a moment of panic in the crowded hallway.

keyWords.definition: to believe that someone is honest and will do what they say
keyWords.example: I trust my best friend to keep my secrets safe.

keyWords.definition: quiet and peaceful, not worried or excited
keyWords.example: Even during the storm, the captain stayed calm and steered the boat safely.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A shepherd's false alarms cost him the village's trust, until honesty earns it back
A village gradually decides that wolves are not dangerous creatures, so it stops guarding
A bored shepherd boy becomes the village's most popular storyteller and is loved by all
A loyal sheepdog slowly teaches the villagers new farming skills over many seasons
questions.why: The story shows how Samir's repeated false alarms made the villagers stop trusting him, and how honesty slowly rebuilt that trust.

wrong.B: The story never claims that wolves are not dangerous.
wrong.C: Samir does not become a popular storyteller.
wrong.D: The sheepdog does not teach the villagers farming skills.

questions.stem: What did the villagers do the first time Samir shouted that a wolf was attacking his sheep?
options: They ignored him and continued their daily work
They quickly sent the sheepdog alone to check on the flock
They dropped their work and rushed up the hill in a panic
They calmly warned Samir never to shout like that again
questions.why: The first time, the villagers believed Samir and rushed up the hill in alarm, only to find no wolf.

wrong.A: They did not ignore him the first time; that happened later.
wrong.B: The villagers themselves rushed up, not just the dog.
wrong.D: No warning like this happens after the very first trick.

questions.stem: How did the villagers' feelings toward Samir change after the first two false alarms?
options: They grew increasingly angry and decided to ignore his warnings
They began to panic every single time they saw Samir
They calmly warned him to leave the flock and move away
They stayed just as calm and trusted him exactly as before
questions.why: The story says the villagers grew tired and angry and eventually decided to ignore Samir's cries altogether.

wrong.B: They did not panic at the mere sight of Samir himself.
wrong.C: No one tells Samir to leave the flock or the village.
wrong.D: Their trust in Samir clearly weakened, not stayed the same.

questions.stem: Why did the villagers ignore Samir's warning the night a real wolf actually came?
options: They were too calm to believe anything bad could happen
They did not trust the sheepdog's loud, panicked barking
They warned each other that wolves never attack at night
They assumed it was another one of his false alarms
questions.why: Because Samir had lied before, the villagers assumed his new warning was simply another trick, so they ignored it.

wrong.A: Their calmness is not the reason they ignored him.
wrong.B: The dog's barking is what eventually changed their minds, not the cause of ignoring him.
wrong.C: The villagers do not make this claim about wolves and nighttime.

questions.stem: What can you infer about the sheepdog from how differently it barked that final evening?
options: It only panics and barks loudly when it wants food
It stays calm and only barks urgently when danger is real
It barks the same way every single day without any reason
It warns the sheep, not the villagers, about any danger
questions.why: Because the dog had never raised a false alarm before, its sudden urgent barking showed that real danger was present.

wrong.A: There is no mention that the dog barks for food.
wrong.C: Its barking that evening was clearly different from usual.
wrong.D: The dog's barking is what alerts the villagers, not just the sheep.

questions.stem: Why did a few villagers finally decide to climb the hill despite doubting Samir?
options: Samir calmly warned them he would pay for their trust
They saw the wolf running fast toward the village itself
It was simply time for their evening meal together
The sheepdog's panicked barking sounded unusually urgent
questions.why: The villagers noticed that the dog's barking sounded far more urgent than usual, which made them decide to check.

wrong.A: Samir does not offer any payment in the story.
wrong.B: The wolf stays near the flock; it does not run toward the village.
wrong.C: Mealtime is never given as a reason in the story.

questions.stem: In the story, what does it mean that the villagers decided to 'ignore' Samir's cries?
options: They chose to pay close attention to every single word
They chose to panic and rush to help him instantly
They chose to pay no attention to what he was saying
They chose to warn him calmly about his past behavior
questions.why: To ignore means to pay no attention to something, which is exactly what the villagers did after Samir's repeated tricks.

wrong.A: Ignoring is the opposite of paying close attention.
wrong.B: The villagers did the opposite of rushing to help.
wrong.D: The story does not describe a calm warning being given here.

questions.stem: How does the story organize Samir's three warnings and the real wolf's arrival?
options: It lists farming steps for raising a healthy flock of sheep
It shows three false alarms, then a real danger that tests trust
It compares Samir's village with a village from long ago
It describes a calm, peaceful day with no problems
questions.why: The story is organized around Samir's two false alarms, followed by a real wolf arriving, which tests whether anyone will still believe him.

wrong.A: The story does not list farming steps.
wrong.C: No other village or time period is compared in the story.
wrong.D: The story centers on real problems, not a calm, problem-free day.

MID.prompt: Explain why the villagers stopped trusting Samir, and how he eventually earned their trust back. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained why the villagers stopped trusting Samir.
I explained how Samir eventually earned their trust back.
I used at least two details from the story.
MID.modelAnswer: The villagers stopped trusting Samir because he tricked them two extra times by shouting about a wolf that was not really there, so they decided to ignore his warnings after that. When a real wolf finally came, nobody believed him at first, and only his dog's urgent barking made a few villagers check the hill. Samir earned their trust back by staying calm and telling the plain truth instead of exaggerating, which slowly showed the village that he could be honest.

keyWords.definition: doubtful about whether something is true or will happen
keyWords.example: The scientist remained skeptical until the experiment's results were checked twice.

keyWords.definition: to give someone false or incorrect information on purpose
keyWords.example: The advertisement seemed designed to mislead customers about the product's true price.

keyWords.definition: watchful and alert, always paying close attention to possible danger
keyWords.example: The night guard stayed vigilant, checking every door and window along his route.

keyWords.definition: a result or effect that happens because of an earlier action
keyWords.example: Forgetting to water the plants had a clear consequence: they slowly wilted.

keyWords.definition: the quality of being believable and trusted by other people
keyWords.example: After admitting his mistake honestly, the manager actually gained more credibility with his team.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Repeated false alarms destroy credibility, which only honesty can slowly restore
Wolves pose no genuine danger to a village's flock of sheep, even at night in winter
A sheepdog proves more capable than any shepherd in the village, so the sheep follow him
Village life stays calm and uneventful until a new shepherd arrives to take over the hills
questions.why: The story centers on how Samir's repeated lies damaged his credibility, and how only sustained honesty slowly earned the village's trust back.

wrong.B: The real wolf in the story shows that danger clearly exists.
wrong.C: The story is not a comparison between the dog's and Samir's abilities.
wrong.D: The village's calm is disrupted repeatedly by Samir's tricks and the real wolf.

questions.stem: Why did the villagers remain skeptical even as Samir called for help the final time?
options: They were vigilant enough to recognize the danger instantly
His earlier deceptions had already destroyed his credibility
The consequence of ignoring him seemed too small to matter
They assumed the sheepdog would mislead them on purpose
questions.why: Because Samir had lied repeatedly before, the villagers no longer found him credible, so they doubted his final, genuine warning.

wrong.A: The villagers were not immediately alert to the real danger; they doubted it at first.
wrong.C: The story does not frame their hesitation around weighing a small consequence.
wrong.D: The dog is shown as reliable, not as something that might mislead anyone.

questions.stem: What ultimately convinced a few villagers to investigate despite their doubts?
options: Samir offered them a generous reward for climbing the hill
They had already spotted the wolf from a safe distance
The unusually urgent, unending barking of the sheepdog
The consequence of staying home felt unbearable
questions.why: The story explains that the dog's unusually urgent and unending barking is what finally made some villagers decide to check.

wrong.A: Samir does not offer any reward in the story.
wrong.B: The villagers had not yet seen the wolf themselves.
wrong.D: No such reasoning about staying home is described.

questions.stem: What does the sheepdog's consistent behavior suggest about why it was trusted when Samir was not?
options: It was simply louder than Samir had ever managed to be
It belonged to the most respected family in the village
It had been specially trained to recognize wolves by sight
It had never once misled anyone with a false alarm
questions.why: Because the dog had always been vigilant and never raised a false alarm, its urgent barking carried real credibility that Samir's words had lost.

wrong.A: The story emphasizes the dog's honesty, not simply its volume.
wrong.B: No family connection or ownership is discussed in the story.
wrong.C: The story never mentions any special training for the dog.

questions.stem: In the story, what does it mean that Samir's actions had 'misled' the village?
options: His actions had given the village false, incorrect information
His actions had calmed the entire village's worries for the night
His actions had warned the village about a real danger nearby
His actions had protected the flock from genuine harm in the hills
questions.why: To mislead means to give someone false information, which is exactly what Samir's fake wolf warnings did to the villagers.

wrong.B: His false alarms created worry, not calm.
wrong.C: His early warnings were about danger that did not exist.
wrong.D: His tricks did not protect anyone, since there was no real threat.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order.
options: A real wolf finally appears, villagers lose trust, Samir lies twice more
Samir lies twice more, villagers lose trust, a real wolf finally appears
Villagers lose trust, Samir lies twice more, a real wolf appears
A real wolf appears, Samir lies twice more, villagers lose trust
questions.why: Samir lies twice more after his first trick, the villagers then lose trust in him, and only afterward does a real wolf finally appear.

wrong.A: The wolf appears only after trust is already lost, not before the extra lies.
wrong.C: The villagers lose trust because of the extra lies, which must come first.
wrong.D: Trust is lost before, not after, the real wolf appears.

questions.stem: What consequence did Samir face as a direct result of his repeated false alarms?
options: The villagers rewarded him with a larger, finer flock
The villagers appointed him leader of the entire village
The villagers refused to believe him when real danger arrived
The villagers gave his loyal sheepdog away to another family
questions.why: Because Samir had lied repeatedly, the direct consequence was that the villagers did not believe his genuine warning when a real wolf appeared.

wrong.A: Samir is not rewarded with a larger flock.
wrong.B: Samir is never appointed as a leader in the story.
wrong.D: The sheepdog remains with Samir throughout the story.

questions.stem: Why does the author have the sheepdog—not Samir—convince the villagers that real danger has arrived?
options: To show that dogs are naturally smarter than every shepherd in the village
To explain exactly how sheepdogs are trained from birth to guard flocks
To prove that Samir's warnings were always correct before this day
To suggest that steady honesty earns trust that careless words cannot
questions.why: By having the ever-honest dog succeed where the lying Samir fails, the author shows that consistent, honest behavior earns trust that careless words cannot.

wrong.A: The point is about honesty, not a general comparison of intelligence.
wrong.B: The story never explains how sheepdogs are trained.
wrong.C: Samir's earlier warnings were false, not correct.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says it is okay to tell a lie as a joke, even if it worries other people. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Samir's lies and their consequences.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that it is okay to tell a lie as a joke, even if it worries other people. Samir's joking lies about a wolf cost him his credibility: after two extra false alarms, the villagers decided to ignore him altogether, and that nearly left him without help on the night a real wolf actually came. Someone might argue that his lies were harmless fun, since no one was ever truly hurt, but the story shows the real consequence was almost far worse: without his vigilant, honest sheepdog, the villagers might never have come at all.

LOW.stem: What did the people carry when they ran up the hill to scare the wolf?
options: Baskets
Sticks
Blankets
Kites
LOW.why: The text says some people ran up the hill with sticks and made a lot of noise.

wrong.A: Baskets are not mentioned.
wrong.C: Blankets are not mentioned.
wrong.D: Kites are not mentioned.

LOW.stem: Why did the people get mad at Samir?
options: He lost all of his sheep.
He took food from them.
He tricked them three times.
He stopped working on the hill.
LOW.why: Each time the people ran up the hill, there was no wolf, so they got mad.

wrong.A: His sheep were safe until the end.
wrong.B: Taking food is not mentioned.
wrong.D: He kept his flock on the hill.

LOW.stem: In the story, the word trust means —
options: to run away from a wolf
to laugh at a funny joke
to feel sad and lonely
to believe in someone
LOW.why: The people did not trust Samir because he had lied, so they did not believe him.

wrong.A: Trust is about believing, not running.
wrong.B: The people were mad, not laughing.
wrong.C: Samir felt lonely, but that is not what trust means.

LOW.stem: How did Samir feel when he sat with the sheep each day?
options: Bored and lonely
Happy and busy
Scared and cold
Angry and hungry
LOW.why: The story says Samir got bored and lonely while he watched the flock on the hill.

wrong.B: He was alone with little to do, so he was not happy and busy.
wrong.C: The story does not say he was scared or cold on the hill.
wrong.D: The story does not say he was angry or hungry.

MID.stem: What does Samir do differently on the evening the real wolf comes?
options: He laughs at the villagers
He runs away from the sheep
He hides behind the dog
He tells the plain truth calmly
MID.why: This time Samir stays calm and speaks the plain truth in a steady voice.

wrong.A: He laughed at the villagers during the earlier tricks.
wrong.B: He stays with the flock.
wrong.C: The dog barks; Samir does not hide.

MID.stem: The story says that this time Samir did not exaggerate. What does exaggerate mean?
options: to whisper very softly
to make a thing sound bigger
to run far away from danger
to tell a friend a secret
MID.why: Before, Samir made up a danger that was not real; this time he told the plain truth, so exaggerate means to make something sound bigger than it is.

wrong.A: Whispering is not exaggerating.
wrong.C: Running away is not what the word means.
wrong.D: Telling a secret is not exaggerating.

MID.stem: Why does Samir first play the trick on the villagers?
options: To break up a dull afternoon
To get help with his flock
To warn them about a wolf
To test his sheepdog
MID.why: In the text, he played the trick just to break the monotony of a dull afternoon.

wrong.B: There was no real danger to the flock yet.
wrong.C: There was no wolf the first time.
wrong.D: The sheepdog is not part of the first trick.

MID.stem: Why does the author say Samir forced himself to stay calm?
options: To show he was afraid of dogs
To show he was very tired
To show he learned honesty
To show the wolf was a joke
MID.why: Samir stops exaggerating and tells the plain truth, which shows he has learned to be honest.

wrong.A: The dog is on his side.
wrong.B: Tiredness is not the point of the phrase.
wrong.D: The wolf is real this time.

HIGH.stem: What drew the real wolf toward the flock?
options: The barking of the dog
The light of the torches
The shouts of the villagers
The scent of the sheep
HIGH.why: In the text, the wolf was drawn by the scent of sheep in the gathering darkness.

wrong.A: The dog barks after the wolf arrives.
wrong.B: The torches come later, with the villagers.
wrong.C: The villagers do not come until later.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word credibility means —
options: the speed of a runner
a feeling of being tired
being easy to believe
the sound of a loud bark
HIGH.why: The villagers were no longer willing to treat his warnings as believable.

wrong.A: The word is about belief, not speed.
wrong.B: The word is about belief, not tiredness.
wrong.D: The barking comes from the dog, and the word is not about sound.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author describe Samir's boredom and solitude at the start?
options: To show he loves his flock
To explain why he played tricks
To say the village was large
To describe the dry weather
HIGH.why: His boredom and loneliness lead him to play the trick to break the monotony.

wrong.A: The text says he was bored and isolated, not delighted.
wrong.C: The village is described as quiet, not large.
wrong.D: The weather is only part of the setting.

HIGH.stem: Why did the villagers stop believing Samir?
options: They could not hear him well
He had tricked them more than once
They were asleep in their homes
They were afraid of wolves
HIGH.why: Samir repeated the trick several times, so the villagers stopped trusting him.

wrong.A: Hearing was not the problem; trust was.
wrong.C: The story does not say they were asleep.
wrong.D: Fear of wolves would make them come, not stay away.
